offence_severity: Minimum 7 years, Maximum 10 years for Section 498A; Minimum 10 years, Maximum 10 years for Section 302
number_of_offences: Two offences charged (Section 498A and 302), both upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the appellant's behavior and actions were part of a pattern of harassment and financial demands
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of four prosecution witnesses clearly proved that the appellant was addicted to consuming liquor, used to demand money from the deceased and her parents, and at times ill-treated and assaulted the deceased. The presence of kerosene oil on the deceased's body and in the room, along with the nature of burn injuries, supported the conclusion that the appellant was responsible for her death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (the father and mother of the deceased) as credible, stating that they are the most natural and material witnesses to speak on such issues. Their evidence was corroborated by their relatives, and there was no contradiction in their testimony despite lengthy cross-examination.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 02.10.1995; Trial judgment: 31.05.2000; High Court decision: 03.01.2007; Supreme Court decision: 07.01.2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Mallikarjun S. Mylar, Manjunath, Ms.Umme Salma, Ms. E. R. Sumathy Advs.; Counsel for the State: Joseph Aristotle S., Mrs.Priya Aristotle, Shiva P., Ms. Aruna Hannah Dutta, Ms. Anitha Shenoy, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant poured kerosene on his wife and set her on fire, resulting in her death. The evidence of four prosecution witnesses clearly proved that the appellant was addicted to liquor, frequently demanded money from the deceased and her parents, and ill-treated and assaulted the deceased. The deceased's death was homicidal, not accidental, and the appellant was the only person present at the time of the incident.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the deceased's sari accidentally caught fire while she was boiling water on the oven, resulting in her death. They claimed it was an accidental death and that the prosecution's case was not sufficiently proven.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the conduct of the accused towards his wife, including repeated harassment, demand for dowry, and ill-treatment, fell within the meaning of Section 498-A IPC. The court also determined that the death was homicidal, not accidental, based on the evidence.
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the evidence clearly proved the appellant's guilt under Sections 498-A and 302 IPC beyond reasonable doubt. The court found that the deceased's death was homicidal and that the appellant was solely responsible for her death.
